The Environment’s Hidden Death Toll

Some deaths make the news. How do they compare with deaths from the environment?

12.6 million deaths a year, nearly 1 in 4 of all deaths worldwide, are attributable to modifiable environmental risks. On a death certificate, they appear under these names.

Environmental deaths are not a separate disease: they are counted inside heart disease, stroke, cancers and other causes.

Part Two
Studying Environmental Health

How do we know what in our surroundings makes us sick?

17.2 · What Is the Study of Environmental Health?

What Is Environmental Health?

Environmental health is the study of human interactions with environmental factors affecting health. Three fields do most of the work:

Toxicology

The study of toxic substances and their effects.

Studies negative effects of substances on organisms. Hatmakers’ ‘erethism’ (1860s). Example: neurological damage from mercury, pioneered by Alice Hamilton in the US.

Epidemiology

Disease patterns and causes in populations.

Studies distribution and causes of disease in populations. John Snow (1854) mapped London cholera cases to public water pumps, founding modern epidemiology.

Public Health

Protecting the health of whole communities.

Study and practice of protecting and improving community health: administers vaccinations, monitors disease, and responds to environmental health crises like COVID-19.

17.3 · How Do Microorganisms Make Us Sick?

Major Types of Biological Hazards

Biological hazards, organic substances that threaten health, account for one in four human deaths. Pathogens take up residence in our bodies to cause illness or infection.

© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
17.3 · DDT: Trading a Biological Hazard for a Chemical One

A Public Health Bargain with Hidden Costs

DDT was a cheap, effective pesticide that became the WHO's plan to eradicate malaria globally in the 1950s, until Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) revealed its broader harms.

DDT persists in the environment, moves up the food chain, and kills birds and other species beyond mosquitoes (a classic example of unintended ecological consequences).

Stockholm Convention (2001): banned DDT for most uses but allowed its continued use for malaria control where safe, effective, and affordable alternatives are unavailable.

This case illustrates the challenge of environmental health trade-offs: solving one hazard can create another.

Food chain: Woodwell, Wurster & Isaacson (1967), Science 156:821–824 (Long Island estuary). Eagles: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (1963 and 2006 nesting pairs; 2018–19 aerial survey, 2021 report).

Part Three
Toxic Exposure

What makes a substance dangerous, and how does it get inside us?

17.4 · What Does It Mean When Something Is Toxic?

The Dose Makes the Poison

Paracelsus (1500s): “the does makes the poison.”

  • All chemicals can be toxic depending on the amount of exposure. Botox (botulin toxin) at 1/667 the lethal dose is a safe medical treatment; at full dose, it kills.
  • Toxicologists measure risk as percent mortality of exposed populations, typically the dose required to kill half (LD50).
Lethal dose (LD50) per kilogram of body weight. Longer bar = more needed to kill = safer.
LD50vs. water
The most poisonous is

Approximate oral LD50s in rats (PubChem); botulinum toxin is the estimated lethal dose for a person by mouth, about 1 µg/kg (Arnon et al. 2001, JAMA); injected, it is roughly a thousand times smaller. Water’s figure is a lower bound.

17.4 · What Impacts Toxicity?

What Impacts Toxicity?

How much harm a chemical does depends on three things: the dose of exposure, duration of exposure, and route of exposure.

Chemical hazards: chemicals linked to immediate or delayed health effects. Toxic chemicals cause injury, death, tissue/organ damage, or disruption of biological functions.
1DoseHow much enters the body.
2DurationMinutes, or decades.
3RouteBreathed, swallowed, or through skin.

Additive toxicity: effects of interacting chemicals sum together.

Part Four
Hazards, Risk, and Vulnerability

The same storm, flood or earthquake can be an inconvenience in one place and a catastrophe in another.

17.7 · Hazard, Risk, and Disaster

Hazard, Risk, and Disaster

The same flood can be a nuisance or a catastrophe. Raise the river, then change the community.

Reduce vulnerability
0homes flooded
0people harmed
HazardA source of potential harm or danger. Here: the flood.
RiskThe likelihood of experiencing harm from a hazard. It depends on the hazard and on who is in its way.
VulnerabilitySusceptibility to harm from hazards. Vulnerable groups are communities lacking resources and support.
DisasterWhen a hazard strikes a vulnerable community and the harm overwhelms its ability to cope.
Reducing the riskReducing vulnerability can be achieved through improved preparedness and planning. To reduce disaster risk: hazard mapping and preparedness programs.

Illustrative model: 12 homes, 4 residents each. Disaster definition after the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR).

17.8 · How Is Climate Change Affecting Environmental Health?

Expanding Hazards, Shrinking Refuges

  • Flooding: storm surges, intense rainfall, and rapid snowmelt, worsened by loss of coastal wetlands that once buffered floodwaters.
  • Heat waves: periods of unusually high temperatures that last days or weeks. Syria's 2006–09 drought displaced 1 million people and contributed to civil war.
  • Expanded disease ranges: tick habitat in the US has expanded by 400+ counties since 1996. West Nile virus incidence expected to rise with warmer, wetter storms.

Part Five
Environmental Justice and Resilience

Who carries the burdens, who shares the benefits, and who gets a say?

17.1 · How Are Environmental Benefits and Burdens Distributed?

Environmental Justice

Environmental justice: fair treatment and meaningful involvement of all people in environmental decision-making.

The concern: pollution is concentrated in disadvantaged communities.

Environmental inequityHigher pollution burdens in low-income neighborhoods.
Environmental equityFair treatment regarding environmental benefits and burdens: an equitable distribution of environmental benefits.
Meaningful involvementCommunities participate in decisions affecting them.
The lines that stayed a composite city, not a real place

Federal appraisers at the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation graded city neighborhoods by mortgage risk. Neighborhoods of color and immigrants were graded D, “hazardous,” and outlined in red, cutting them off from home loans.

Interstates, rail yards and industry were often routed through the lowest-graded neighborhoods, where land was cheap and residents had little say. Parks and street trees went to the A neighborhoods.

Eight decades later, the same lines still show up in the heat, the trees and the air.

+2.6°Chotter land surface on summer days in formerly redlined neighborhoods, on average across 108 U.S. citiesHoffman et al. 2020
23% vs 43%tree canopy in D-graded neighborhoods vs A-graded, on average across 37 metro areasLocke et al. 2021

17.6 · Dumping Toxic Burdens on Developing Countries

Bhopal, India, 1984

A chemical plant accident at a US company's (Union Carbide) pesticide facility in Bhopal exposed 500,000+ residents to poisonous gas, causing 10,000+ deaths.

The plant operated in India to produce pesticides for sale, under weaker regulatory oversight than would have applied in the US.

Union Carbide accepted moral responsibility, paying $554 million to survivors, averaging $2,200 per person for injuries including blindness, respiratory illness, and death.

Bhopal remains the world's worst industrial disaster and a defining case study in environmental justice, corporate responsibility, and the global export of hazardous industry.

An illustration, not a map. The settlements beside the plant were among the hardest hit.

© 2023 W. W. Norton & Company, Inc.
17.9 · Community Resilience

Community Resilience

Community resilience is a community’s ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from challenges. It is strengthened by social networks and community cooperation.

Improved by (switch them on)

Switch on a measure to see what it does.

Environmental justice and resilience: fair access to resources helps communities better withstand and recover from environmental challenges.

A circular economy keeps materials in use. Communities benefit through reduced landfill use and resource extraction.

lowest point
to recover
losses vs. no measures

A disaster strikes at the red line. Resilience is two things: how far the community falls, and how fast it gets back up. The shaded area is everything lost along the way: homes, jobs, schooling, health care.

Illustrative model of the “resilience triangle”: how far a community’s functioning drops after a shock, and how long it takes to recover. The dashed line is the same community with none of the measures.

Chapter 17 · Key Concepts

Environmental Health and Justice

Environmental Justice
No community should bear more environmental burdens than others
Epidemiology
Study of disease distribution and determinants in populations
Toxicology
Study of negative effects of substances on organisms
Biological Hazard
Organic substance threatening the health of living organisms
Persistent Organic Pollutants
Chemicals that resist breakdown and accumulate in food chains
Synergistic Toxicity
Combined chemical effects greater than their individual sum
Herd Immunity
Community protection when most members are vaccinated
Precautionary Principle
EU standard: restrict chemicals until proven safe, not vice versa
Hazard
A source of potential harm or danger
Risk
The likelihood of experiencing harm from a hazard
Vulnerability
Susceptibility to harm from hazards
Community Resilience
A community's ability to prepare for, respond to, and recover from challenges
